items.title: Family Law Rules
items.says: The Family Law Rules apply to family law cases in the Family Court of the Superior Court of Justice, the Superior Court of Justice and the Ontario Court of Justice, including cases under the Divorce Act, the Family Law Act and the Children's Law Reform Act.

source.expect: These rules apply to all family law cases

review.problem: r. 1(2) only says which family cases and courts the rules apply to; it says nothing about the rules setting out steps, forms and deadlines.

items.title: Family Law Act
items.says: Under the Family Law Act, when spouses divorce, their marriage is declared a nullity, or they separate with no reasonable prospect of living together again, the spouse with the smaller net family property is entitled to one-half the difference between the two.

source.expect: net family property

review.problem: FLA s. 5(1) is only the equalization entitlement; support, the matrimonial home, domestic contracts and restraining orders are in other Parts of the Act.

items.title: Children's Law Reform Act
items.says: Part III of the Children's Law Reform Act deals with decision-making responsibility, parenting time, contact and guardianship for children, decided on the basis of the children's best interests; it also aims to avoid competing cases in more than one place, discourage child abduction and enforce parenting and contact orders.

source.expect: The purposes of this Part are

review.problem: CLRA s. 19 sets out the purposes of Part III (decision-making responsibility, parenting time, contact, guardianship by best interests, jurisdiction, abduction, enforcement); it does not mention parentage or say the Act applies when parents are not divorcing or not married.

items.title: Divorce Act
items.says: Under the federal Divorce Act, a court may grant a divorce, on the application of either or both spouses, on the ground that the marriage has broken down.

source.expect: grant a divorce to the spouse or spouses

review.problem: Divorce Act s. 8(1) only gives the court power to grant a divorce on the ground of marriage breakdown; parenting orders and support are in other sections.

items.title: Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996
items.says: Under this Ontario law, the Director (the Family Responsibility Office) must enforce support orders that are filed in the Director's office, along with any related support deduction order, and pay what is collected to the person it is owed to.

source.expect: enforce support orders

review.problem: s. 5(1) only states the Director's duty to enforce filed support orders and pay out what is collected; it does not set up the office or list support deduction orders, default hearings or licence suspension.

items.title: Federal Child Support Guidelines
items.says: The objectives of the Federal Child Support Guidelines are a fair standard of support so children keep benefiting from both spouses' means after separation, less conflict through more objective calculation, a more efficient legal process, and consistent treatment of similar families.

source.expect: to establish a fair standard of support for children

review.problem: s. 1 states the Guidelines' objectives; it does not say they apply to support ordered under the Divorce Act (that comes from the definition of 'Act' in s. 2(1)).

items.title: Child Support Guidelines (Ontario)
items.says: The objectives of Ontario's Child Support Guidelines are a fair standard of support so children benefit from their parents' financial means, more objective calculation to reduce conflict, guidance that makes the legal process more efficient, and consistent treatment of families in similar circumstances.

source.expect: to establish a fair standard of support for children

review.problem: s. 1 states the regulation's objectives; it does not say it applies to support ordered under the Family Law Act or to parents who never married.

items.title: Courts of Justice Act
items.says: The Courts of Justice Act creates a branch of the Superior Court of Justice called the Family Court.

source.expect: Family Court

review.problem: CJA s. 21.1(1) only creates the Family Court branch of the Superior Court of Justice; it says nothing about setting up the other courts or the Office of the Children's Lawyer.

items.title: Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017
items.says: The Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017 sets out when a child is in need of protection, for example where the child has suffered physical harm caused by the person in charge of the child, or there is a risk the child will suffer it.

source.expect: child is in need of protection

review.problem: CYFSA s. 74(2) defines when a child is in need of protection; it says nothing about children's aid societies running the case, the Family Law Rules, or child protection being separate from disputes between family members.

items.title: Spousal Support Advisory Guidelines
items.says: The Spousal Support Advisory Guidelines are a federal Justice Department publication that gives ranges for the amount and length of spousal support. They are not a law. Courts in Ontario often refer to them.

source.citation: Spousal Support Advisory Guidelines (Department of Justice Canada, July 2008)
source.expect: advisory

items.title: Choosing the right court
items.says: In the parts of Ontario where the Family Court has jurisdiction, the family proceedings listed in the Schedule to section 21.8 of the Courts of Justice Act (other than appeals and prosecutions) must be started, heard and decided in the Family Court.

source.expect: shall be commenced, heard and determined in the Family Court

review.problem: CJA s. 21.8(1) only says that in Family Court areas the scheduled proceedings (except appeals and prosecutions) are started and heard in the Family Court; 'all family matters', the residence test and the split between the Superior Court and the Ontario Court of Justice elsewhere are not in it.

items.title: Family Court branch of the Superior Court
items.says: In the parts of Ontario where the Family Court branch of the Superior Court of Justice has jurisdiction, the family proceedings listed in the Schedule to section 21.8 of the Courts of Justice Act, except appeals and prosecutions, must be started, heard and decided in the Family Court.

source.expect: In the parts of Ontario where the Family Court has jurisdiction

review.problem: Drops the exception in s. 21.8(1): appeals and prosecutions are not required to be started and heard in the Family Court.

items.title: Ontario Court of Justice cannot divide property
items.says: For dividing property under Part I of the Family Law Act, the word "court" does not include the Ontario Court of Justice.

source.expect: does not include the Ontario Court of Justice

review.problem: s. 4(1) only excludes the Ontario Court of Justice from 'court' for Part I (family property); matrimonial home claims are Part II, and which court they go to is not stated in s. 4(1).

items.title: Matrimonial home claims are not in the Ontario Court of Justice
items.says: For the matrimonial home rules in Part II of the Family Law Act, "court" also does not include the Ontario Court of Justice.

source.expect: does not include the Ontario Court of Justice

items.title: Who can get a divorce in Ontario
items.says: An Ontario court can hear a divorce if either spouse has lived habitually in Ontario for at least one year right before the case starts.

source.expect: habitually resident in the province for at least one year

items.title: When an Ontario court can make a parenting order
items.says: Under the Children's Law Reform Act, an Ontario court can make a parenting order if the child is habitually resident in Ontario when the application is started, or in some other cases listed in the Act.

source.expect: the child is habitually resident in Ontario

items.title: Where the case starts (municipality)
items.says: A case starts in the municipality where a party lives. If the case is about decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact for a child, it starts where the child ordinarily lives, with some exceptions.

source.expect: in the municipality where a party resides

items.title: Mandatory Information Program
items.says: In most cases about parenting, property, the matrimonial home, support or a restraining order, and in most motions to change, each party must attend a Mandatory Information Program no later than 45 days after the case is started. The applicant books their own session and gets an appointment for the respondent. Until their attendance certificate is filed, a party cannot take any step except that a respondent can serve and file an answer and a party can book a case conference.

source.expect: no later than 45 days after the case is started

items.title: Cases that do not need the information program
items.says: The information program rule does not apply to some people and cases, including cases proceeding on consent, cases where the only claims are for a divorce, costs or putting an agreement or earlier order into an order, international child abduction cases, and parties who have already attended a program. A motion to change that deals only with child or spousal support is not covered by the rule.

source.expect: Subrules (4) to (7) do not apply to

items.title: Starting a case: the application
items.says: A person starts a family case by filing an application in one of the forms the rule lists (Form 8, 8A, 8B, 8B.1, 8B.2, 8C, 8D, 8D.1, 33D.1, 34L or 34N). When it is filed, the clerk sets a court date (except where the case management rules say otherwise) and seals the application.

source.expect: To start a case, a person shall file an application

review.problem: r. 8(1) only lists the application forms; what each form is for is not stated there, and r. 8(4) has the clerk set a court date (with case-management exceptions) and seal the application, saying nothing about a case conference date or issuing.

items.title: Form 8: Application (General)
items.says: Form 8 is one of the application forms that rule 8(1) lists for starting a family case.

source.expect: To start a case, a person shall file an application (Form 8

review.problem: r. 8(1) only lists Form 8 among the application forms; it does not say Form 8 is the general application or which cases it is used for.

items.title: Form 8A: Application (Divorce)
items.says: Either spouse can start a divorce case by filing an application naming the other spouse as respondent, or both spouses can file a joint application with no respondent.

source.expect: filing a joint application with no respondent

review.problem: r. 36(1) does not mention Form 8A; it only says either spouse may start a divorce case naming the other as respondent, or by a joint application with no respondent.

items.title: Form 8B: Application (Child Protection and Status Review)
items.says: Form 8B is one of the application forms that rule 8(1) lists for starting a family case.

review.problem: r. 8(1) only lists Form 8B among the application forms; it does not say who uses it or that it starts a child protection case.

items.title: Affidavit for parenting claims (Form 35.1)
items.says: An application, answer or motion to change that claims decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact must be served and filed with an affidavit in Form 35.1, and also Form 35.1A if the child or a party has been involved with a child protection agency.

source.expect: an affidavit in Form 35.1

items.title: Automatic order when a parenting, property or support claim is made
items.says: When a claim about decision-making responsibility or parenting time, net family property, the matrimonial home, or support is made (in an application, answer, motion to change or response), the clerk issues an automatic order (Form 8.0.1). It is served with the application, or within seven days if the claim is in a later document. It is not issued in a case proceeding on consent.

source.expect: the clerk shall issue an automatic order (Form 8.0.1)

items.title: Serving the application
items.says: The application must be served right away on every other party, by special service unless the party is one of the officials, agencies or others listed in rule 8(6).

source.expect: shall be served immediately on every other party

review.problem: r. 8(5) requires immediate special service except on the listed officials and agencies, but the description of what special service is comes from r. 6(3), not r. 8.

items.title: What counts as special service
items.says: Special service includes leaving a copy with the person, leaving it with their lawyer who accepts service in writing, and mailing it to the person with an acknowledgment of service (Form 6) that is signed and returned.

source.expect: special service

items.title: Proving service (Form 6B)
items.says: Service can be proved in several ways, including a written acceptance of service, an affidavit of service (Form 6B), the signed return postcard, or a lawyer's or paralegal's certificate of service (Form 6C).

source.expect: affidavit of service

review.problem: r. 6(19) says service may be proved by any of several methods, of which an affidavit of service (Form 6B) is one; it does not say the affidavit is signed by the person who served.

items.title: Substituted service or no service
items.says: The court can order a document served by substituted service, by a method the court chooses, if the party asking gives detailed evidence of the steps taken to locate and serve the person and shows the method could reasonably be expected to bring the document to the person's attention.

source.expect: substituted service

review.problem: States the trigger as 'not practical to serve in the usual way'; r. 6(15) instead requires detailed evidence of steps taken to locate and serve and a method reasonably expected to bring the document to the person's attention, and 'service not needed' is r. 6(16), not 6(15).

items.title: Financial statement with the application
items.says: A party who claims support, property or exclusive possession of the matrimonial home serves and files a financial statement with the document that contains the claim (Form 13 for support only, Form 13.1 if there is a property or matrimonial home claim); the other party serves and files one within the time for responding. A claim only for table-amount child support does not need one, unless the rules require it.

source.expect: shall serve and file a financial statement

review.problem: Drops the r. 13(1.3) exception: a party whose only support claim is table-amount child support does not have to file a financial statement, and the responding party files within the time for answering, not with the claim document.

items.title: Form 13: Financial Statement (Support Claims)
items.says: Form 13 is the financial statement for a case that has a support claim but no property claim.

source.expect: shall be in Form 13

items.title: Form 13.1: Financial Statement (Property and Support Claims)
items.says: Form 13.1 is the financial statement for a case that has a property claim, with or without a support claim.

source.expect: shall be in Form 13.1

items.title: Financial statement in a property claim
items.says: A party in a case with a property claim must serve and file a financial statement in Form 13.1, even if there is no support claim.

source.expect: shall be in Form 13.1, whether a claim for support

items.title: Respondent's financial statement
items.says: The party against whom a support, property or matrimonial home claim is made serves and files a financial statement within the time for serving and filing an answer (or a response to the motion), whether or not they serve an answer.

source.expect: within the time for serving and filing an answer

items.title: Respondent's answer: 30 days
items.says: A respondent serves an answer (Form 10, or the child protection or adoption form that applies) on every other party and files it within 30 days after being served with the application.

source.expect: within 30 days after being served with the application

review.problem: The 60-day period for service outside Canada or the U.S. is r. 10(2), not 10(1); r. 10(1) also lists other answer forms (33B, 33B.1, 33B.2, 33D.3).

items.title: Answer time when served outside Canada or the U.S.
items.says: If the application was served outside Canada or the United States, the respondent has 60 days to serve and file an answer.

source.expect: the time for serving and filing an answer is 60 days

items.title: Making a claim in the answer
items.says: A respondent can include their own claim in the answer, against the applicant or against another person, who then also becomes a respondent.

source.expect: a claim against the applicant

items.title: Reply: 10 days
items.says: A party can serve and file a reply (Form 10A) within 10 days after being served with an answer, to respond to a claim made in the answer.

source.expect: within 10 days after being served with an answer

items.title: If no answer is filed
items.says: If a respondent does not serve and file an answer, the consequences in rule 1(8.4) apply: the respondent is not entitled to further notice of steps (except service of the order), cannot take part in the case, the court can deal with the case in their absence, and a date can be set for an uncontested trial.

source.expect: if a respondent does not serve and file an answer

items.title: Amending an application or answer
items.says: A party can amend an application or answer without permission in some situations, for example before an answer is filed. Otherwise the court gives permission unless the change would hurt another party in a way that costs or an adjournment cannot fix.

source.expect: the court shall give permission to a party to amend

items.title: Withdrawing a claim
items.says: A party can withdraw all or part of their application, answer or reply by serving a notice of withdrawal (Form 12) on every other party and filing it. The withdrawing party pays the other parties' costs of the withdrawn part up to the date of withdrawal, unless the court orders or the parties agree otherwise. A special party or child party needs the court's permission to withdraw.

source.expect: notice of withdrawal

review.problem: r. 12(3) says a withdrawing party shall pay the other parties' costs up to the withdrawal unless the court orders or the parties agree otherwise, not merely that costs 'can' follow; and a special party's or child party's claim can be withdrawn only with the court's permission (r. 12(2)).

items.title: Consequences of not following the rules or an order
items.says: When the court strikes out a party's application, answer, motion to change or response, then unless the court orders otherwise the party is not entitled to further notice of steps (except service of the order), cannot take part in the case, the court can deal with the case in their absence, and a date can be set for an uncontested trial.

source.expect: not entitled to any further notice

review.problem: r. 1(8.4) applies when a party's application, answer, motion to change or response is struck out; not answering at all is covered by r. 10(5), not r. 1(8.4).

items.title: Order when a party does not follow the rules or an order
items.says: If a person does not follow the rules or an order, the court can make any order it considers necessary for a just outcome, including dismissing a claim, striking documents, making a costs order, or ordering a party to pay money.

source.expect: the court may deal with the failure by making any order

items.title: Uncontested trial
items.says: At an uncontested trial, evidence can be given by affidavit in Form 14A or Form 23C (and Forms 35.1 and 35.1A where they apply) without a separate order, unless the court directs that oral evidence must be given.

source.expect: uncontested trial

review.problem: r. 23(22) only says which affidavit evidence (Form 14A or 23C, and 35.1/35.1A if applicable) can be used at an uncontested trial without an order, unless the court directs oral evidence; it says nothing about when an applicant can ask for an uncontested trial.

items.title: Form 23C: Affidavit for Uncontested Trial
items.says: Form 23C is the affidavit a party uses to give the facts and evidence the judge needs at an uncontested trial.

source.expect: evidence by affidavit in Form 14A or Form 23C

items.title: Certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A)
items.says: A party who must serve support or property disclosure documents under rule 13 confirms it by serving a certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A) with the documents, and files it no later than six days (applicant or moving party) or four days (other party) before a case conference.

source.expect: certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A)

items.title: Net family property statement (Form 13B)
items.says: Before a settlement conference or trial, each party to a Family Law Act property claim serves and files a net family property statement (Form 13B), or an affidavit saying an earlier statement has not changed.

source.expect: a net family property statement (Form 13B)

items.title: Comparison of net family property statements (Form 13C)
items.says: Parties who have served net family property statements file a joint comparison of net family property statements (Form 13C) no later than six days before a settlement conference. If they cannot agree on a joint one, each files their own, six days (requesting party) or four days (other party) before.

source.expect: joint comparison of net family property statements (Form 13C)

items.title: Updating a financial statement
items.says: Before a conference, motion or trial, a party updates their financial information if their last financial statement would be more than 60 days old at a case or settlement conference, more than 30 days old at a motion, or more than 40 days old at trial. They serve and file an affidavit saying nothing changed, an affidavit with minor changes, or a new financial statement.

source.expect: a party shall update their financial information

items.title: Asking for more financial information
items.says: A party who thinks the other party's financial disclosure is not enough first asks for the missing information in writing. If it is not given within seven days, the court can, on motion or at a case or settlement conference, order the other party to give it or to serve and file a new financial statement.

source.expect: does not provide enough information for a full understanding

items.title: Statement of property in an equalization claim
items.says: In an application for equalization under section 7 of the Family Law Act, each party serves and files a sworn statement of their property, debts and other liabilities as of the date of marriage, the valuation date and the date of the statement.

source.expect: each party shall serve on the other and file with the court

items.title: Affidavit listing documents
items.says: Within 10 days after another party asks, each party gives that party an affidavit listing every document that is relevant to any issue in the case and that the party controls or can get on request. This does not apply to documents already required under the financial disclosure rule.

source.expect: within 10 days after another party’s request

items.title: Documents held by someone not in the case
items.says: If a relevant document is in the control of someone who is not a party, is not privileged, and it would be unfair to a party to go on without it, the court can, on a motion served on the parties and on the non-party by special service, order the non-party to let the party see it and supply a copy.

source.expect: If a document is in a non-party’s control

items.title: Questioning (out-of-court examination)
items.says: Outside child protection cases, a party can question another party or get information by affidavit only with the other party's consent or a court order. The court can order it if it would be unfair to go on without it, the information is not easily available another way, and it will not cause unacceptable delay or undue expense.

source.expect: It would be unfair to the party who wants the questioning

items.title: Request to admit (Form 22)
items.says: A party can ask another party to admit facts or that a document is genuine. If the other party does not respond within 20 days, they are taken to admit them.

source.expect: request to admit

items.title: Office of the Children's Lawyer
items.says: In a Divorce Act or Children's Law Reform Act case about decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact, the Children's Lawyer may investigate, or meet with the child to learn the child's views and preferences, and may report and make recommendations to the court. The Children's Lawyer may do this on their own initiative, at the court's request or at anyone's request.

source.expect: cause an investigation to be made on all matters

review.problem: CJA s. 112 lets the Children's Lawyer investigate, meet the child to learn the child's views and preferences, and report; it does not say the Children's Lawyer acts as the child's legal representative.

items.title: Children's Lawyer report and disputing it
items.says: When the Children's Lawyer investigates, it serves a notice, then serves and files its report within 90 days. A party who disagrees can serve and file a statement disputing the report within 30 days after being served with it. There is no trial or final order until those 30 days pass, unless the parties give up that time.

source.expect: within 30 days after being served with the report

items.title: Court-ordered parenting assessment
items.says: The court can appoint a person with technical or professional skill to assess the needs of the child and the ability and willingness of the parties to meet them, and to report to the court.

source.expect: appoint a person

items.title: Case conference
items.says: In each case where an answer is filed, a judge holds at least one conference (in child protection cases a case conference is optional, and the rule does not apply to international child abduction cases). The purposes of a case conference include exploring settlement, identifying the issues in dispute, ensuring disclosure and setting the next steps.

source.expect: a judge shall conduct at least one conference

review.problem: r. 17 does not contain the bar on serving or hearing motions before a conference on the substantive issues (that is in rule 14); r. 17(1) also has exceptions for child protection and international child abduction cases.

items.title: What a case conference is for
items.says: The purposes of a case conference include exploring settlement, identifying the issues that are in dispute and those that are not, making sure disclosure is made, and setting a timetable for the case.

source.expect: exploring the chances of settling the case

items.title: Case conference brief and timing
items.says: Each party serves and files a case conference brief (Form 17A, or 17B in child protection). The party who asked for the conference (or the applicant) does this no later than six days before the conference, and the other party no later than four days before.

source.expect: not later than six days before the date scheduled

items.title: Confirmation of conference (Form 17F)
items.says: Each party gives every other party a copy of the confirmation of conference (Form 17F), except in a child protection case, and then gives it to the clerk no later than 2 p.m. three days before the conference.

source.expect: confirmation of conference (Form 17F)

review.problem: The consequence of not confirming is r. 17(14.1), not 17(14); 17(14)(b) also excepts child protection cases from giving the other party a copy.

items.title: Settlement conference
items.says: A settlement conference is held to try to settle or narrow the issues, make sure there is disclosure, and, if possible, get a view of how the court might decide the case. Each party serves and files a settlement conference brief (Form 17C, or 17D in child protection). A case is not scheduled for trial until a settlement conference has been held, unless a judge orders it.

source.expect: settling or narrowing the issues in dispute

items.title: Trial management conference
items.says: A trial management conference is held to get the case ready for trial: how evidence will be received, the witnesses, how long the trial will take and the trial date. In the Ontario Court of Justice each party files a trial management conference brief (Form 17E). In the Superior Court, parties file the trial scheduling endorsement form, an offer to settle and an outline of their opening statement.

source.expect: deciding how the trial will proceed

items.title: Settlement conference judge does not hear the trial
items.says: A judge who conducts a settlement conference about an issue cannot hear that issue, except in a child protection case where the need for protection was found without a trial and a trial is needed only on which order to make.

source.expect: shall not hear the issue

review.problem: r. 17(24) has no exception for the parties' agreement; the only exception (r. 17(25)) is for certain child protection trials.

items.title: Orders a judge can make at a conference
items.says: At a conference a judge can, if the conditions apply, make orders such as disclosure orders, temporary or final orders on consent, and orders to move the case along.

source.expect: At a case conference, settlement conference or trial management conference the judge may

items.title: Motions: asking for a temporary order
items.says: A party asks the court for a temporary order (for example temporary support or parenting) or directions by motion. A motion needs a notice of motion (Form 14) and an affidavit (Form 14A), or a motion form (Form 14B) if it is only about procedural, uncomplicated or unopposed matters.

source.expect: requires a notice of motion (Form 14) and an affidavit

items.title: No motion before a case conference, except urgent
items.says: Until a conference dealing with the substantive issues has been completed, no motion can be served or heard, unless the court finds urgency or hardship or that a case conference is not required for another reason in the interest of justice. Some motions are not covered by this bar, such as motions made without notice, on consent, unopposed or by Form 14B, contempt motions, summary judgment motions and motions in child protection cases.

source.expect: urgency or hardship

review.problem: Drops the r. 14(6) list of motions the bar does not apply to (for example motions on consent, unopposed or Form 14B motions, motions without notice, contempt, summary judgment and child protection motions), so 'cannot bring a motion' overstates the rule.

items.title: Motion without notice
items.says: A motion can be made without notice if notice is unnecessary or not reasonably possible; if there is an immediate danger that a child will be removed from Ontario, or to the health or safety of a child or the moving party, and the delay of serving notice would probably have serious consequences; or if serving notice would probably have serious consequences.

source.expect: A motion may be made without notice if

review.problem: Drops the condition in r. 14(12)(b) and (c) that the delay of serving notice would probably have serious consequences; an immediate danger alone is not enough.

items.title: Evidence on a motion
items.says: An affidavit for a motion (usually Form 14A) is to contain, as much as possible, only facts the person knows personally. It can include information learned from someone else only if the source is named and the person says they believe it is true.

source.expect: only information within the personal knowledge

items.title: Confirmation of motion (Form 14C)
items.says: The moving party gives every other party a copy of the confirmation of motion (Form 14C), subject to the child protection exception in r. 14(11.0.1), and then gives it to the clerk no later than 2 p.m. three days before the motion date.

source.expect: confirmation of motion (Form 14C)

review.problem: The consequence of not confirming is r. 14(11.1), not 14(11).

items.title: Form 14B: Motion Form
items.says: If a motion is limited to procedural, uncomplicated or unopposed matters, the party making it may use a motion form (Form 14B) instead of a notice of motion and affidavit.

source.expect: a motion form (Form 14B) instead of a notice of motion

review.problem: r. 14(10) only lets a party use Form 14B instead of a notice of motion and affidavit for procedural, uncomplicated or unopposed matters; it does not say such motions are dealt with on the documents.

items.title: Costs of a motion
items.says: Promptly after dealing with each step in a case, such as a motion, the court decides in a summary way who, if anyone, is entitled to costs and the amount, or expressly reserves costs to a later step.

source.expect: Promptly after dealing with a step in a case

items.title: Offer to settle (Form 18)
items.says: A party can serve an offer to settle any claim, at any time, even before the case starts. The offer must be signed personally by the party making it and by their licensed representative, if they have one.

source.expect: signed personally by the party

items.title: Accepting an offer
items.says: The only valid way to accept an offer is to serve an acceptance on the party who made it before the offer is withdrawn or the court begins to give a decision on a claim in the offer. An offer can still be accepted even after it was rejected or a counter-offer was made.

source.expect: The only valid way of accepting an offer

items.title: Cost consequences of an offer
items.says: Unless the court orders otherwise, a party who made an offer is entitled to costs up to the date the offer was served and full recovery of costs after that, if the offer was made at least one day before a motion (or seven days before a trial or other hearing), did not expire and was not withdrawn, was not accepted, and the party got an order as good as or better than the offer. The party claiming this must prove it.

source.expect: full recovery of costs from that date

items.title: Costs: the successful party
items.says: Except as the rule provides, there is a presumption that a successful party is entitled to the costs of a step in a case. If success is divided, the court can split costs. The presumption does not apply in child protection cases.

source.expect: presumption that a successful party is entitled to the costs

items.title: Unreasonable behaviour and costs
items.says: A successful party who behaved unreasonably during a step can lose all or part of their own costs or be ordered to pay the other party's costs. The court can look at their behaviour, whether they made an offer to settle, how reasonable it was, and any offer they withdrew or did not accept.

source.expect: has behaved unreasonably during a step

items.title: Bad faith and full recovery costs
items.says: If a party has acted in bad faith, the court must decide costs on a full recovery basis and order the party to pay them right away.

source.expect: shall decide costs on a full recovery basis

items.title: Factors for setting costs
items.says: In setting the amount of costs for a step, the court can consider the reasonableness and proportionality of each party's behaviour, the time spent, written offers to settle, legal fees, expert fees and other expenses, compared with the importance and complexity of the issues. Fees claimed must be supported by documents.

source.expect: the reasonableness and proportionality of the following

items.title: Summary judgment
items.says: After the respondent has served an answer or the time for an answer has passed, a party can make a motion for summary judgment, a final order without a trial on all or part of any claim or defence. This is available in any case that does not include a divorce claim, including a child protection case.

source.expect: summary judgment

review.problem: Drops r. 16(2)-(3): summary judgment is available only in a case that does not include a divorce claim; in a divorce case the uncontested divorce procedure or splitting the divorce claim is used instead.

items.title: Test for summary judgment
items.says: The court makes a final order if there is no genuine issue requiring a trial of a claim or defence. The judge can weigh evidence, judge credibility and draw inferences to decide that.

source.expect: no genuine issue requiring a trial

items.title: Trial record
items.says: At least 20 days before the trial (or trial sittings), the applicant serves and files a trial record with a table of contents and the documents listed in the rule, such as the application, answer and reply, updated financial documents and temporary orders. A respondent can add documents up to seven days before trial.

source.expect: At least 20 days before the earlier of the start

items.title: Trial
items.says: At trial, the judge hears the evidence of the parties and their witnesses and decides the issues. A party can call the opposing party as a witness. Evidence can be given by affidavit or another method only if the court orders it and it is served at least 30 days before trial.

source.expect: served at least 30 days before the start of the trial

items.title: Summons to witness
items.says: A party who wants a witness to give evidence or bring documents serves a summons to witness (Form 23) by special service, with the witness fee, at least seven days before the witness is needed.

source.expect: shall serve on the witness a summons to witness (Form 23)

items.title: The order
items.says: The party in whose favour the court makes an order prepares a draft of it (Form 25, 25A, 25B, 25C or 25D), unless the court orders otherwise.

source.expect: shall prepare a draft of the order

items.title: Settling by consent
items.says: If the parties agree, the court can make an order under the rules or an Act without the parties or anyone else coming to court.

source.expect: without having the parties or any other person come to court

review.problem: r. 25(1) only lets the court make an order on consent without anyone coming to court; Form 14B and the consent motion to change (Forms 15C and 15D) are not mentioned in rule 25.

items.title: Filing a domestic contract for enforcement
items.says: A person can file a domestic contract that has support terms with the court clerk, and the support terms can then be enforced, and changed, as if they were an order of the court.

source.expect: may file the contract with the clerk

items.title: Ground for divorce: breakdown of marriage
items.says: The only ground for divorce is breakdown of the marriage. It is shown by living separate and apart for at least one year before the divorce judgment, or by adultery, or by physical or mental cruelty that makes living together intolerable.

source.expect: Breakdown of a marriage is established only if

items.title: Living separate and apart
items.says: Spouses are separate and apart if they lived apart and one of them intended to do so. Living together again for up to 90 days to try to reconcile does not stop the time running.

source.expect: not more than ninety days with reconciliation as its primary purpose

items.title: Simple or joint divorce
items.says: When the respondent does not answer, or in a joint application, the divorce can be granted on affidavit evidence. The applicant files an affidavit for divorce (Form 36) confirming the application, with child support information, a draft divorce order (Form 25A) and stamped envelopes, plus the marriage certificate and the report from the Central Registry of Divorce Proceedings. The clerk sends the file to a judge.

source.expect: An affidavit in Form 36

items.title: Court must be satisfied about child support
items.says: The court must stay (put on hold) the divorce if it is not satisfied that reasonable arrangements have been made for the support of any children of the marriage under the applicable guidelines.

source.expect: reasonable arrangements have been made for the support

items.title: Collusion and reconciliation
items.says: The court must satisfy itself that there was no collusion in the divorce application, and must dismiss the application if it finds there was collusion in presenting it.

source.expect: collusion

review.problem: s. 11(1)(a) only requires the court to dismiss the application if it finds collusion; the duty to consider the possibility of reconciliation is in s. 10(1), not s. 11.

items.title: When a divorce takes effect: 31 days
items.says: Subject to the rest of section 12, a divorce takes effect on the 31st day after the day the judgment granting it is rendered.

source.expect: a divorce takes effect on the thirty-first day

review.problem: The earlier-date exception is s. 12(2), not s. 12(1).

items.title: Certificate of divorce
items.says: After the divorce takes effect, either spouse can get a certificate of divorce from the court office.

source.expect: certificate

items.title: Removing barriers to religious remarriage
items.says: A spouse can file an affidavit saying the other spouse controls a barrier to the deponent's religious remarriage. If the other spouse does not show within 15 days that the barriers have been removed, the court can dismiss applications filed by that spouse and strike out their other pleadings.

source.expect: within fifteen days after that affidavit is filed

items.title: Duties of parties in a divorce
items.says: To the extent it is appropriate, parties to a Divorce Act proceeding must try to resolve the matters that could be the subject of an order through a family dispute resolution process.

source.expect: family dispute resolution process

review.problem: Divorce Act s. 7.3 only sets the duty to try a family dispute resolution process where appropriate; the best-interests, protection-from-conflict and information duties are separate sections (7.1, 7.2, 7.4), and the information duty applies only 'if required to do so under this Act'.

items.title: Parenting orders: decision-making and parenting time
items.says: A court can make a parenting order about parenting time or decision-making responsibility for a child of the marriage, on the application of either or both spouses, or of another person who is a parent of the child or stands or intends to stand in a parent's place; that other person needs the court's leave to apply.

source.expect: may make an order providing for the exercise of parenting time

review.problem: s. 16.1(1) does not define decision-making responsibility (that is s. 2(1)), and it allows applications by a spouse or by a non-spouse parent or person standing in a parent's place, who needs the court's leave (s. 16.1(3)); 'to one or more parents or others' is not in it.

items.title: Parenting order under the Children's Law Reform Act
items.says: A parent can apply for a parenting order about decision-making responsibility and parenting time. A person who is not a parent, such as a grandparent, can apply for a parenting order about decision-making responsibility, or for a contact order. The application comes with an affidavit setting out the applicant's proposed plan for the child and other required information.

source.expect: parenting order

review.problem: Under CLRA s. 21 a non-parent can apply for a parenting order only about decision-making responsibility (not parenting time), and the section requires no leave of the court for a non-parent.

items.title: Best interests of the child (Children's Law Reform Act)
items.says: In making a parenting or contact order, the court considers only the best interests of the child. It gives primary consideration to the child's physical, emotional and psychological safety, security and well-being, and considers all factors about the child's circumstances, including those listed in the Act.

source.expect: shall only take into account the best interests of the child

items.title: Best interests of the child (Divorce Act)
items.says: Under the Divorce Act, the court considers only the best interests of the child, with primary consideration for the child's physical, emotional and psychological safety, security and well-being.

source.expect: only the best interests of the child

items.title: Best-interests factors
items.says: The listed factors include the child's needs and stage of development, the child's relationships with each parent and others, each parent's willingness to support the child's relationship with the other parent, the history of care, the child's views and preferences, cultural and religious upbringing, any plans for the child's care, each person's ability to care for the child, and any family violence.

source.expect: the child's views and preferences

items.title: Parenting time consistent with best interests
items.says: The court is to give effect to the principle that a child is to have as much time with each parent as is consistent with the best interests of the child.

source.expect: as much time with each parent as is consistent

items.title: Family violence and parenting
items.says: Family violence is defined broadly: conduct by a family member toward another that is violent or threatening, is a pattern of coercive and controlling behaviour, or causes fear for someone's safety, and for a child includes direct or indirect exposure to it. It includes physical, sexual, psychological and financial abuse, threats, harassment and stalking, and need not be a criminal offence.

source.expect: family violence

review.problem: CLRA s. 18 defines family violence (with the list in s. 18(2)); the court's consideration of its nature, seriousness, frequency and effect on the child is in s. 24(4), not s. 18.

items.title: Family violence definition (Divorce Act)
items.says: The Divorce Act defines family violence as conduct by a family member toward another family member that is violent or threatening, that is a pattern of coercive and controlling behaviour, or that causes the other person to fear for their safety or that of another person.

source.expect: coercive and controlling behaviour

items.title: Past conduct
items.says: The court does not consider a person's past conduct unless it is relevant to their parenting of the child.

source.expect: past conduct

items.title: Parenting plan
items.says: The court includes in a parenting order or contact order any written parenting plan the parties submit, for the parts they agree on, with any changes the court considers in the child's best interests.

source.expect: written parenting plan submitted by the parties

items.title: Contact order for others
items.says: A person other than a parent, such as a grandparent, can apply to the court for a contact order with a child.

source.expect: contact order

review.problem: CLRA s. 21(3) lets any non-parent, including a grandparent, apply for a contact order; it does not require the court's permission (leave).

items.title: Supervised parenting time or contact
items.says: The court can give directions for supervision of decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact by a person, a children's aid society or another body, but only if that person or body agrees to act as supervisor.

source.expect: for the supervision, by a person, a children’s aid society

items.title: Notice of a proposed relocation
items.says: A person with decision-making responsibility or parenting time who plans to move with the child in a way that could significantly affect the child's relationship with another person must give written notice at least 60 days before the move, with the planned date and new address.

source.expect: at least 60 days before the expected date

items.title: Notice of relocation (Divorce Act)
items.says: Under the Divorce Act, a person planning to relocate a child must give notice at least 60 days before, in the form required by regulations.

source.expect: at least 60 days before the expected date

items.title: Objecting to a relocation: 30 days
items.says: Under the Children's Law Reform Act, a person with decision-making responsibility or parenting time who receives notice of a proposed relocation can object no later than 30 days after receiving it, by sending a written objection or by starting a court application.

source.expect: no later than 30 days after receiving the notice

items.title: Deciding whether to allow a relocation
items.says: In deciding whether to allow a relocation, the court considers the best interests factors plus the reasons for the move, its effect on the child, the time each person spends with the child, whether notice was given, any existing order or agreement, whether the proposal for new parenting time is reasonable, and whether each party has followed their obligations. It does not consider whether the person would move without the child.

source.expect: the reasons for the relocation

items.title: Burden of proof in relocation
items.says: If the parties substantially comply with an order, arbitral award or agreement providing that the child spends substantially equal time with each party, the party who wants to relocate the child must prove the move is in the child's best interests. If they substantially comply with one providing that the child spends the vast majority of time with the moving party, the party opposing must prove it is not. In any other case, the parties share the burden of proving whether the move is in the child's best interests.

source.expect: substantially equal time

review.problem: s. 16.93 turns on the parties substantially complying with an order, arbitral award or agreement that provides for equal time or for the vast majority of time with the moving party, not on how time is actually spent; it also omits s. 16.93(3) for other cases.

items.title: Relocation factors (Children's Law Reform Act)
items.says: The Children's Law Reform Act has the same relocation factors and burdens for cases that are not under the Divorce Act.

source.expect: the reasons for the relocation

items.title: Wrongful removal of a child
items.says: The Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction, set out in the Schedule to section 46 of the Children's Law Reform Act, has been in force in Ontario since December 1, 1983, and its provisions are law in Ontario.

source.expect: Convention

review.problem: CLRA s. 46(2) only brings the Hague Convention into force in Ontario; it says nothing about the court ordering a child returned or police locating the child (those are other CLRA provisions).

items.title: Police help to locate and deliver a child
items.says: If the court is satisfied there are reasonable and probable grounds to believe that someone is unlawfully withholding a child from a person entitled to decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact, or that someone is about to remove the child from Ontario against a court order or separation agreement (or a person with parenting time or contact proposes to remove the child and the child would probably not be returned), the court can direct a police service to locate, apprehend and deliver the child. The application can be made without notice if the court is satisfied that action must be taken without delay.

source.expect: direct a police service

review.problem: s. 36(3) allows the application without notice only where the court is satisfied that action must be taken without delay; the condition is dropped.

items.title: Every parent must support their child
items.says: Every parent must support their unmarried child, to the extent the parent is capable, if the child is a minor, is enrolled in a full-time program of education, or cannot withdraw from the parents' charge because of illness, disability or other cause. The obligation does not extend to a child 16 or older who has withdrawn from parental control.

source.expect: to the extent that the parent is capable of doing so

review.problem: Drops s. 31(1)(c) (a child unable to withdraw from parental charge because of illness, disability or other cause) and the s. 31(2) exception: the obligation does not extend to a child 16 or older who has withdrawn from parental control.

items.title: Child support table amount
items.says: Unless the Guidelines say otherwise, the amount of child support for children under the age of majority is the table amount for the paying parent's income and number of children, plus any special or extraordinary expenses.

source.expect: the amount set out in the applicable table

items.title: Child support table amount (Ontario)
items.says: The Ontario Guidelines have the same rule: the table amount based on the paying parent's income, plus special or extraordinary expenses.

source.expect: the amount set out in the applicable table

items.title: Special or extraordinary expenses (section 7)
items.says: The court can order a share of special or extraordinary expenses, such as child care, health costs not covered, extra education costs, post-secondary education and extracurricular activities, considering whether they are necessary and reasonable. They are usually shared in proportion to the parents' incomes.

source.expect: provide for an amount to cover all or any portion of the following expenses

items.title: Children over the age of majority
items.says: For a child who is 18 or older, the amount is the table amount as if the child were under 18, unless that is inappropriate, in which case the court considers the child's condition, means, needs and other circumstances.

source.expect: the age of majority or over

items.title: Shared parenting (40% rule)
items.says: When each parent has the child at least 40% of the time over a year, child support is decided considering the table amounts for each parent, the higher costs of shared parenting, and each parent's means and needs.

source.expect: not less than 40% of parenting time

items.title: Split custody
items.says: When each parent has one or more children living mostly with them, each pays the other the table amount and the difference is the amount owed.

source.expect: difference between the amount

items.title: Income over $150,000
items.says: When the paying spouse's income is over $150,000, the amount is the usual table amount under section 3; if the court considers that inappropriate, it is the table amount on the first $150,000, plus for the rest of the income an amount the court considers appropriate given the children's circumstances and each spouse's ability to contribute, plus any special or extraordinary expenses.

source.expect: is over $150,000

review.problem: Under s. 4 the amount is the ordinary s. 3 amount (full table) unless the court considers it inappropriate; only then is it the table amount on the first $150,000 plus an amount the court considers appropriate on the balance, plus any s. 7 expenses.

items.title: Undue hardship
items.says: The court can order a different amount if the parent or child would otherwise suffer undue hardship, for example because of unusually high debts or access costs or support for other people. The court must also compare the standards of living of the two households, and cannot change the amount if the claiming household would have a higher standard of living.

source.expect: undue hardship

items.title: Determining income
items.says: Subject to sections 17 to 20, a parent's annual income is worked out from the sources of income listed under "Total income" in the T1 General tax form, adjusted as Schedule III sets out.

source.expect: Total income

review.problem: s. 16 refers to the sources of income under the heading 'Total income' in the T1 General form (no line number), and the three-year pattern of income is s. 17, not s. 16.

items.title: Imputing income
items.says: The court can impute income to a parent, for example if the parent is intentionally under-employed or unemployed, is not using property reasonably, or has failed to give income information.

source.expect: intentionally under-employed or unemployed

items.title: Income information for child support
items.says: A parent whose income is used to set child support must provide income tax returns, notices of assessment, recent pay statements and other listed documents.

source.expect: income tax return

items.title: Yearly income disclosure
items.says: Once a year, on written request, a parent paying support must give updated income information to the other parent.

source.expect: once a year

items.title: Retroactive child support
items.says: When a recipient asks to increase child support for a past period, they must first show a past material change in circumstances. A presumption then arises in favour of increasing support back to the date the payor got effective notice, up to three years before formal notice of the application. The court can depart from this date in some cases.

source.expect: up to three years before formal notice of the application

items.title: Applying for child support under the Family Law Act
items.says: A court can, on application, order a person to support their dependants. Under the Family Law Act, an application for a child's support can be made by the child (the dependant) or the child's parent, and in some cases by a social assistance agency.

source.expect: order a person to provide support for his or her dependants

items.title: Online Child Support Service and recalculation
items.says: In Ontario, parents can use the Child Support Service to set up or recalculate child support without going to court, if they qualify.

source.expect: Child Support Service

items.title: Spousal support obligation
items.says: Every spouse has an obligation to support themselves and the other spouse, according to need, to the extent they are capable of doing so.

source.expect: in accordance with need

items.title: Who is a spouse for support (common law)
items.says: For support, "spouse" includes two people who are not married but have lived together continuously for at least three years, or who are in a relationship of some permanence and are the parents of a child.

source.expect: continuously for a period of not less than three years

items.title: Factors for spousal support (Family Law Act)
items.says: In deciding spousal support, the court considers the spouses' means and needs, and factors such as age and health, the length of cohabitation, contributions to the relationship, the effect of child care on earning capacity, and the goal of financial independence.

source.expect: the dependant's and respondent's current assets and means

items.title: Purposes of spousal support (Family Law Act)
items.says: The purposes of a spousal support order are to recognize contributions to the relationship and the economic results of it, share the economic burden of child support fairly, help a spouse become able to contribute to their own support, and relieve financial hardship.

source.expect: recognize the spouse's contribution to the relationship

items.title: Spousal support under the Divorce Act
items.says: Under the Divorce Act, the court can order spousal support after considering the condition, means, needs and other circumstances of each spouse, including how long they lived together, their roles during the relationship, and any order or agreement about support.

source.expect: condition, means, needs and other circumstances

items.title: Objectives of spousal support (Divorce Act)
items.says: The objectives of a spousal support order are to recognize economic advantages or disadvantages from the marriage or its breakdown, share the financial consequences of caring for children, relieve economic hardship from the breakdown, and promote each spouse's economic self-sufficiency within a reasonable time.

source.expect: economic self-sufficiency of each spouse within a reasonable period

items.title: Misconduct and spousal support
items.says: Under the Divorce Act, the court does not consider misconduct of a spouse in relation to the marriage when deciding spousal support.

source.expect: shall not take into consideration any misconduct

items.title: Child support comes first
items.says: When there is both a child support and a spousal support claim, the court gives priority to child support.

source.expect: give priority to child support

items.title: No limitation period for Family Law Act support claims
items.says: There is no limitation period for a proceeding to get support under the Family Law Act, or to enforce a support or maintenance term in a contract or agreement that could be filed under section 35 of that Act.

source.expect: a proceeding to obtain support under the Family Law Act

review.problem: The parenthetical about FLA s. 50 being repealed is not in Limitations Act s. 16(1) (it is shown in the FLA itself).

items.title: Equalization of net family property
items.says: When a marriage ends by divorce or separation with no reasonable prospect of resuming cohabitation, the spouse with the smaller net family property is entitled to one-half of the difference between the two net family properties.

source.expect: one-half the difference between them

items.title: Net family property
items.says: Net family property is the value of all property a spouse owns on the valuation date, other than excluded property, minus the spouse's debts and liabilities, and minus the value of property (other than a matrimonial home) owned on the date of marriage after deducting the debts on that date, not counting debts directly related to acquiring or significantly improving a matrimonial home.

source.expect: net family property

review.problem: Drops the exception for excluded property under s. 4(2) and the rule that date-of-marriage debts related to acquiring or significantly improving a matrimonial home are not deducted, both of which change the calculation.

items.title: Valuation date
items.says: The valuation date is usually the date the spouses separated with no reasonable prospect of resuming cohabitation, or the divorce date or the day before one spouse's death, if earlier.

source.expect: no reasonable prospect that they will resume cohabitation

items.title: Excluded property
items.says: Some property owned on the valuation date is not included in net family property, such as gifts or inheritances from a third person after the marriage (other than a matrimonial home), damages for personal injury, life insurance proceeds, and property the spouses agreed in a domestic contract to exclude.

source.expect: does not form part of the spouse's net family property

items.title: Proving deductions and exclusions
items.says: The person who claims a deduction or an exclusion must prove it.

source.expect: The onus of proving a deduction

items.title: Unequal division
items.says: The court can award more or less than half the difference if equalizing would be unconscionable, considering things like a failure to disclose debts, debts incurred recklessly, a short marriage, or intentional or reckless depletion of property.

source.expect: unconscionable

items.title: Time limits for an equalization claim
items.says: An equalization application under section 5(1) or (2) cannot be brought after the earliest of two years after the marriage ends by divorce or judgment of nullity, six years after the spouses separate with no reasonable prospect of resuming cohabitation, and six months after the first spouse's death.

source.expect: two years after the day the marriage is terminated by divorce

review.problem: s. 7(3) has no power to extend the time (that is FLA s. 2(8)); it also covers a judgment of nullity alongside divorce and counts six months from the first spouse's death.

items.title: Extending the time for a property claim
items.says: The court can extend the time for an equalization claim if there are apparent grounds for relief, the delay was in good faith, and no one will suffer substantial prejudice because of it.

source.expect: apparent grounds for relief

items.title: Orders the court can make in a property case
items.says: The court can order payment of the equalization amount, security for it, payment in instalments for up to 10 years, transfer of property, partition or sale.

source.expect: be paid in instalments during a period not exceeding ten years

items.title: Preservation order
items.says: If a spouse's claim may be defeated, the court can make an order restraining the depletion of a spouse's property that would impair or defeat a claim.

source.expect: restraining the depletion

items.title: Unjust enrichment and trust claims (unmarried spouses)
items.says: In Kerr v. Baranow, the Supreme Court said that when the parties were engaged in a joint family venture and the claimant's contributions are linked to building up wealth, a money award for unjust enrichment is calculated as a share of the accumulated wealth proportionate to the claimant's contributions; the first step is to identify whether there was a joint family venture.

source.expect: joint family venture

review.problem: Kerr para. 87 does not discuss unmarried spouses' lack of an equalization claim or trusts; it says that where the parties were in a joint family venture and the claimant's contributions are linked to the generation of wealth, the monetary award is a share of the accumulated wealth proportionate to the claimant's contributions.

items.title: Dividing a pension
items.says: The value of a pension is included in net family property, and the court can order a lump sum transfer from the plan, subject to the rules in the Act and the Pension Benefits Act.

source.expect: imputed value

items.title: What a matrimonial home is
items.says: A matrimonial home is every property in which a person has an interest and that is or was, at the time of separation, ordinarily occupied by the person and their spouse as their family residence.

source.expect: ordinarily occupied by the person and his or her spouse as their family residence

items.title: Equal right to possession
items.says: Both spouses have an equal right to possession of a matrimonial home. If only one spouse has an interest in it, the other spouse's right of possession is personal against the first spouse and ends when they stop being spouses, unless a separation agreement or court order provides otherwise.

source.expect: an equal right to possession of a matrimonial home

review.problem: Under s. 19(2), where only one spouse has an interest in the home, the other spouse's right of possession is personal against the first spouse and ends when they cease to be spouses unless a separation agreement or court order provides otherwise; it does not last 'until' an agreement or order.

items.title: Selling or mortgaging the home needs consent
items.says: Neither spouse can sell or mortgage a matrimonial home without the other spouse's consent, unless the other has released their rights or a court order permits it.

source.expect: No spouse shall dispose of or encumber an interest in a matrimonial home

items.title: Exclusive possession of the matrimonial home
items.says: The court can order that one spouse have exclusive possession of the home, considering the best interests of the children, existing orders, the spouses' finances, written agreements, the availability of other accommodation, and any violence committed by a spouse against the other spouse or the children.

source.expect: any violence committed by a spouse against the other spouse or the children

items.title: Designating a matrimonial home
items.says: One or both spouses can designate property as a matrimonial home in the prescribed form and register the designation. When a designation made by both spouses is registered, any other matrimonial home not designated by both stops being a matrimonial home; a designation registered by one spouse alone leaves the other matrimonial homes in place.

source.expect: designate

review.problem: Under s. 20(4)-(5), other matrimonial homes stop being matrimonial homes only when a designation made by both spouses is registered; if one spouse alone registers a designation, other matrimonial homes remain matrimonial homes.

items.title: Domestic contracts
items.says: Marriage contracts, cohabitation agreements, separation agreements, paternity agreements and family arbitration agreements are domestic contracts.

source.expect: marriage contract

items.title: Formal requirements
items.says: A domestic contract must be in writing, signed by the parties and witnessed, or it cannot be enforced.

source.expect: made in writing, signed by the parties and witnessed

items.title: Setting aside a domestic contract
items.says: A court can set aside a domestic contract or part of it if a party failed to disclose significant assets or debts, did not understand its nature or consequences, or on any other contract-law ground.

source.expect: failed to disclose to the other significant assets

items.title: Contract terms about children
items.says: The court can disregard a term about the education, moral training or parenting of a child if it is not in the child's best interests.

source.expect: best interests of the child

items.title: Overriding a support waiver
items.says: The court can set aside a waiver of spousal support in a domestic contract and order support if the waiver results in unconscionable circumstances, or the person qualifies for public assistance, or there is a default under the contract.

source.expect: unconscionable circumstances

items.title: Restraining order (Family Law Act)
items.says: The court can make a restraining order against a spouse or former spouse, or a person who lived with the applicant, if the applicant has reasonable grounds to fear for their own safety or the safety of a child in their lawful custody.

source.expect: reasonable grounds to fear for his or her own safety

items.title: Restraining order (Children's Law Reform Act)
items.says: In a parenting case, the court can make a restraining order on the same test, against any person, if the applicant has reasonable grounds to fear for their safety or the safety of a child in their lawful care.

source.expect: restraining order

items.title: Breaking a restraining order

items.title: Motion to change a final order or agreement

items.says: A party served with a motion to change who does not agree, or who wants a different change, serves and files a response to motion to change (Form 15B). items.title: Changing an order on consent

items.title: Change in circumstances: child support
items.says: Before changing a child support order under the Divorce Act, the court must be satisfied that a change of circumstances as defined in the Child Support Guidelines has happened since the order or the last change.

source.expect: a change of circumstances as provided for in the applicable guidelines

items.title: Changing a parenting order

source.expect: change in the circumstances of the child

items.title: Reducing or rescinding arrears

items.title: Changing a Family Law Act support order

source.expect: material change in the dependant's or respondent's circumstances

items.title: Appeal from the Ontario Court of Justice
items.says: An appeal from an order of the Ontario Court of Justice under this Part of the Family Law Act goes to the Superior Court of Justice; an appeal from an order of the Family Court of the Superior Court of Justice under this Part goes to the Divisional Court.

source.expect: An appeal from an order of the Ontario Court of Justice

source.expect: within 30 days after the date of the order or decision being appealed from

items.title: Appeal from the Superior Court
items.says: An appeal goes to the Divisional Court from a final order of a Family Court judge made only under an Ontario Act or regulation, from certain final orders of a Superior Court judge described in the Act, and, with leave, from an interlocutory (temporary) order of a Superior Court judge.

items.title: Appeal under the Divorce Act

items.title: Stay of the order pending appeal

source.expect: does not stay a support order

items.title: Filing with the Family Responsibility Office

items.title: Withdrawing from the Family Responsibility Office
items.says: A support order filed with the Family Responsibility Office can be withdrawn at any time by written notice, signed by the recipient and the payor if the payor is in compliance, or by the recipient alone if the payor is not, unless the order says it cannot be withdrawn. items.title: Default hearing
items.says: When a support order filed with the Family Responsibility Office is in default, the Director can serve the payor with a statement of arrears and a notice requiring a financial statement, proof of income and an appearance in court to explain the default. items.title: Default hearing under the rules

items.title: Driver's licence suspension

items.title: Motion to refrain from licence suspension

source.expect: refrain from directing the suspension

items.title: Credit bureau reporting

items.title: Garnishment

source.expect: notices of garnishment (Form 29A or 29B)

items.title: Writ of seizure and sale

items.title: Statement of money owed

source.expect: A statement of money owed shall be in Form 26

items.title: Financial examination
items.says: If a payment order is in default, the recipient can serve a request for a financial statement (Form 27) on the payor, who must send a completed financial statement within 15 days. The recipient can also ask an income source for information or hold a financial examination.

source.expect: a recipient may serve a request for a financial statement (Form 27)

items.title: Contempt of a family order
items.says: An order other than a payment order can be enforced by a contempt motion in the case where it was made. The notice of contempt motion (Form 31) and supporting affidavit are served by special service by leaving a copy with the person.

source.expect: may be enforced by a contempt motion

items.title: Contempt of Ontario Court of Justice orders
items.says: In addition to its other contempt powers, the Ontario Court of Justice can punish wilful contempt of or resistance to its process, rules or orders under the Family Law Act (other than restraining orders under section 46) by a fine of up to $5,000, imprisonment of up to 90 days, or both.

source.expect: wilful contempt

items.title: Support across provinces and countries
items.says: Support orders can be registered and enforced, and support applications made, between Ontario and other provinces or countries through the Interjurisdictional Support Orders Act, 2002.

source.citation: Interjurisdictional Support Orders Act, 2002, S.O. 2002, c. 13
source.expect: reciprocating jurisdiction

items.title: Case management
items.says: In the Family Court of the Superior Court of Justice, applications covered by rule 39 (except those in subrule (7)) and motions to change a final order or agreement are fast track cases. items.says: In the Family Court of the Superior Court of Justice, the clerk serves a notice of approaching dismissal (Form 39) by mail or email if the case has not been settled, withdrawn, or scheduled or adjourned for trial before the 365th day after it started, unless that time was lengthened by order.

items.title: Avoiding dismissal
items.says: Within 60 days after the notice, a party can avoid dismissal by getting an order lengthening the time, filing a signed agreement with a motion for an order, withdrawing all claims, scheduling or adjourning the case for trial, or arranging a case conference or settlement conference for the first available date.

source.expect: within 60 days after the notice is served

items.title: Frivolous, vexatious or abusive cases (rule 1.4)
items.says: The court can, on its own or on a party's request (Form 1.4), stay or dismiss a case or motion that appears on its face to be frivolous or vexatious or otherwise an abuse of the court process. source.expect: frivolous or vexatious or otherwise an abuse of the court process

items.title: Vexatious litigant order
items.says: A judge of the Superior Court of Justice or the Court of Appeal who is satisfied that a person has persistently and without reasonable grounds started vexatious proceedings, or conducted a proceeding in a vexatious way, can order that the person may not start new proceedings, or continue earlier ones, in any court without leave of a Superior Court judge. source.expect: persistently and without reasonable grounds

items.title: The primary objective of the rules
items.says: The primary objective of the rules is to enable the court to deal with cases justly: fair procedure, saving time and expense, dealing with the case in ways that fit its importance and complexity, and giving resources to the case appropriately.

source.expect: to deal with cases justly

items.title: Counting days
items.says: Days are counted by leaving out the first day and including the last day. If the last day falls on a day the court offices are closed, the time ends on the next day they are open.

source.expect: The first day is the day after the first event

items.title: Lengthening or shortening a time
items.says: The court can lengthen or shorten any time set by the rules or an order, on terms. The parties can agree in writing to lengthen some times.

source.expect: may make an order to lengthen or shorten any time

items.title: Family arbitration and mediation
items.says: Family arbitrations, family arbitration agreements and family arbitration awards are governed by the Family Law Act and the Arbitration Act, 1991; if the two conflict, the Family Law Act prevails.

source.expect: family arbitration

items.title: Gordon v. Goertz
items.says: The Supreme Court of Canada set out the two-step approach for changing a custody order when a parent wants to move: first a material change in circumstances, then a fresh look at the child's best interests. The relocation sections of the Divorce Act now set out much of this test.

items.title: Barendregt v. Grebliunas
items.says: The Supreme Court of Canada restated the law on relocation applications, including how the court considers the best interests of the child and that family violence is relevant to parenting.

source.expect: whether relocation is in the best interests of the child

items.title: Michel v. Graydon
items.says: In Michel v.
